laser-001.question: Which correctly describes the photon emitted by stimulated emission?
choices: It has the same frequency as the incident photon, but its direction and phase are random
The incident photon becomes two photons, each with half its energy
It has the same frequency, phase, direction and polarization as the incident photon
laser-001.explanation: When a photon whose energy equals the energy difference between two levels meets an atom in the upper level, it prompts the atom to drop to the lower level and emit a photon in exactly the same state as the incident one — same frequency, phase, direction and polarization. This is stimulated emission: the incident light is amplified with its properties unchanged, which is the origin of the monochromaticity, directionality and coherence of laser light. Random direction and phase are properties of spontaneous emission, which dominates the light from an LED. Splitting into two photons with half the energy each is parametric down-conversion in nonlinear optics, a different phenomenon from stimulated emission.

laser-002.question: For a transition at 1064 nm (photon energy about 1.17 eV), which value is closest to the ratio N₂/N₁ of atoms in the upper and lower levels in thermal equilibrium at 300 K? (Ignore degeneracy and take kT ≈ 0.0259 eV.)
choices: About 1 (roughly equal numbers above and below)
About 10⁻²⁰
About 10⁻²
laser-002.explanation: In thermal equilibrium the Boltzmann distribution gives N₂/N₁ = exp(−ΔE/kT). Since ΔE/kT = 1.17 / 0.0259 ≈ 45, N₂/N₁ ≈ e⁻⁴⁵ ≈ 2.9×10⁻²⁰: there are almost no atoms in the upper level. About 1 is the limit at very high temperature (kT ≫ ΔE), which thermal equilibrium can only approach; it does not hold for visible or near-infrared transitions at room temperature. About 10⁻² is a miscalculation of the exponential. In thermal equilibrium N₂ < N₁ always, so light is absorbed and attenuated. Laser oscillation requires artificially creating a population inversion, N₂ > N₁, by pumping from outside.

laser-003.question: Why can a steady-state population inversion (N₂ > N₁) not be obtained in a pure two-level system, even when it is excited with intense light?
choices: Because absorption and stimulated emission occur with equal probability, so even strong pumping only brings the populations toward N₂ = N₁
Because spontaneous emission does not occur in a two-level system, so excited atoms pile up without emitting and no light for lasing is obtained
Because the upper level of a two-level system has an infinitely long lifetime, so atoms once excited never return to the lower level
laser-003.explanation: In a two-level system, the pump light drives upward absorption and downward stimulated emission with the same probability (Einstein coefficients B₁₂ = B₂₁, no degeneracy). However hard you pump, net absorption stops once the populations are equal (absorption saturation), and inversion is never reached. That is why three- and four-level systems are used, in which pumping goes to a separate higher level that relaxes quickly to the upper laser level. Spontaneous emission does occur in a two-level system, and the upper level does not have an infinite lifetime. Semiconductor lasers create the inversion by current injection rather than light.

laser-004.question: Why do four-level lasers such as Nd:YAG reach a lower lasing threshold more easily than three-level lasers such as ruby?
choices: Because in a four-level system the lower laser level is the ground state itself, so inversion forms without exciting more than half the atoms
Because the lower laser level lies above the ground state and empties quickly, so even slight pumping creates a population inversion
Because stimulated emission does not occur in a four-level system, so losses are small
laser-004.explanation: In a three-level system (ruby), the lower level of the laser transition is the ground state itself, so creating an inversion requires pumping more than half the ground-state atoms, which makes the threshold high. In a four-level system (Nd:YAG), the lower level lies above the ground state, and atoms that fall into it relax quickly to the ground state, so it stays nearly empty. An inversion therefore exists as soon as there are even a few atoms in the upper level. The option saying “the lower laser level is the ground state” describes a three-level system, the opposite of a four-level one. Stimulated emission is the laser action itself in a four-level system too; without it there would be no lasing.

laser-005.question: An optical resonator is made with two concave mirrors, each with a radius of curvature of 1 m. Which range of mirror spacing L makes the resonator stable (0 ≤ g₁g₂ ≤ 1 with g = 1 − L/R)?
choices: 1 m < L < 2 m
laser-005.explanation: For a symmetric resonator, g₁ = g₂ = 1 − L/R, so g₁g₂ = (1 − L)² (with L in meters). This is at most 1 for 0 ≤ L ≤ 2 m; the end points L = 0 (nearly planar) and L = 2R (concentric resonator) are the stability boundaries. For example, at L = 1.5 m, g = −0.5 and g₁g₂ = 0.25, which is stable, but at L = 2.5 m, g₁g₂ = 2.25, an unstable resonator in which rays move farther from the axis on each round trip. “0 < L < 1 m” mistakes L = R (the confocal resonator) for the upper limit, and “1 m < L < 2 m” misses the lower half. The confocal arrangement has the lowest diffraction loss, and its optical axis also shifts little when a mirror is tilted.

laser-006.question: Which value is closest to the longitudinal mode spacing in wavelength of a Fabry–Perot semiconductor laser (wavelength 1550 nm) that is 300 µm long with a group index of 3.6? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 2.2 nm
About 4.0 nm
About 1.1 nm
laser-006.explanation: The longitudinal mode spacing in frequency is Δν = c/(2n_gL) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 3.6 × 300×10⁻⁶) ≈ 139 GHz. In wavelength, Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (1550×10⁻⁹)² × 139×10⁹ / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 1.1 nm. About 2.2 nm ignores the round trip and uses c/(n_gL); about 4.0 nm takes the group index as 1. Because the gain bandwidth spans tens of nanometers, many longitudinal modes tend to lase at once in this type of laser, and in long-distance communication chromatic dispersion distorts the waveform. DFB and DBR lasers use a grating to select a single mode.

laser-007.question: Which value is closest to the Rayleigh range zR of a Gaussian beam with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a beam waist radius w₀ = 0.5 mm?
choices: About 0.24 m
About 74 mm
About 0.74 m
laser-007.explanation: The Rayleigh range is zR = πw₀²/λ = π × (0.5×10⁻³)² / (1064×10⁻⁹) ≈ 0.74 m. At a distance zR from the waist the beam radius has grown by √2 (the cross-sectional area has doubled), and the range ±zR is where the beam can be regarded as nearly collimated (the confocal parameter, 2zR). About 0.24 m forgets to multiply by π, and about 74 mm is an order-of-magnitude error in unit conversion. Because zR is proportional to w₀ squared, halving the waist cuts the Rayleigh range to 1/4. This is why the depth of focus becomes sharply shallower when a smaller spot is used in laser machining.

laser-008.question: Which value is closest to the far-field half-angle divergence θ of a Gaussian beam (M² = 1) with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a beam waist radius w₀ = 0.5 mm?
choices: About 0.68 mrad
About 2.1 mrad
About 0.34 mrad
laser-008.explanation: The far-field half-angle divergence of a Gaussian beam is θ = λ/(πw₀) = 1064×10⁻⁹ / (π × 0.5×10⁻³) ≈ 6.8×10⁻⁴ rad, or about 0.68 mrad. It can also be written with the Rayleigh range as θ = w₀/zR. About 2.1 mrad is λ/w₀ without dividing by π, and about 0.34 mrad halves the value by confusing the full angle with the half-angle (the full angle is 2θ, about 1.4 mrad). The product of waist radius and divergence, w₀θ = λ/π, is constant, so a narrower beam spreads more. This is the benchmark for beam quality; for real beams the product is M² times larger.

laser-009.question: A 1.064 µm beam (radius w = 5 mm, a nearly collimated Gaussian beam) is focused by a lens with a focal length of 100 mm. Which value is closest to the beam waist radius at the focus? (w₀' ≈ λf/(πw), no aberrations.)
choices: About 21 µm
About 6.8 µm
About 0.68 µm
laser-009.explanation: When a nearly collimated Gaussian beam is focused by a lens of focal length f, the waist radius is w₀' ≈ λf/(πw) = 1.064×10⁻⁶ × 0.1 / (π × 5×10⁻³) ≈ 6.8×10⁻⁶ m, or about 6.8 µm (about 14 µm in diameter). About 21 µm forgets to divide by π, and about 0.68 µm is an order-of-magnitude error. The basic ways to shrink the spot are to shorten the focal length or to enlarge the input beam (with a beam expander). However, the smaller the spot, the shallower the depth of focus (2zR = 2πw₀'²/λ), which here is about 0.27 mm. For a beam with M² greater than 1, the spot radius grows by that factor too.

laser-010.question: Which correctly describes a Gaussian beam at a distance of one Rayleigh range zR from its waist?
choices: The beam radius is twice the waist, and the wavefront is flat
The beam radius is √2 times the waist, and the wavefront radius of curvature is at its minimum, 2zR
The beam radius equals the waist, and the wavefront radius of curvature is infinite
laser-010.explanation: The radius of a Gaussian beam is w(z) = w₀√(1 + (z/zR)²), so at z = zR it is √2 w₀. The wavefront radius of curvature is R(z) = z(1 + (zR/z)²): infinite (a flat wavefront) at the waist (z = 0), approaching z far away, and at its minimum value of 2zR at z = zR. The beam radius doubles at z = √3 zR, and the wavefront is not flat there either. The radius equal to the waist with a flat wavefront describes the position z = 0. In addition, the beam picks up an extra phase of π as it passes through the waist (the Gouy phase), which sets the frequencies of a resonator's transverse modes.

laser-011.question: A single-mode fiber laser with M² (beam quality factor) of 1.1 and a multimode laser with M² of 11 (same beam diameter and wavelength) are focused with the same lens. Which correctly gives the ratio of their focused spot radii?
choices: The multimode spot is about 10 times larger
The multimode spot is about 100 times larger
M² affects only the divergence, so both spots are the same size
laser-011.explanation: For a real beam, the product of waist radius and divergence (the beam parameter product, BPP) is M² times that of an ideal Gaussian beam: BPP = M²λ/π. When beams of the same diameter are focused with the same lens, the spot radius is w₀' ≈ M²λf/(πw), proportional to M², so the ratio is 11/1.1 = 10. About 100 times confuses this with the ratio of spot areas (M² squared); the power per unit area (intensity) is about 1/100. M² sets both the divergence and the spot size at once, not just one of them. Compared at the same spot size, the depth of focus is also shallower in inverse proportion to M².

laser-012.question: Which correctly pairs Q-switching and mode locking with their typical pulse durations?
choices: Q-switching gives femtoseconds, mode locking gives milliseconds
Both give microseconds; only the repetition rate differs
Q-switching gives nanoseconds, mode locking gives picoseconds to femtoseconds
laser-012.explanation: Q-switching pumps the gain medium while the resonator loss is held high, storing energy, then suddenly lowers the loss to release it all at once. The pulse duration is a few resonator round-trip times, typically a few to a few tens of nanoseconds. Mode locking fixes the phases of many longitudinal modes so that they interfere to form a single short pulse circulating in the resonator; the wider the gain bandwidth, the shorter the pulse, reaching picoseconds to femtoseconds (around 10 fs is possible with Ti:sapphire). There is no femtosecond Q-switching or millisecond mode locking. Microseconds for both is closer to the time scale of free-running lamp-pumped operation.

laser-013.question: Which value is closest to the pulse repetition rate of a mode-locked laser with a 1.5 m resonator (a linear resonator in air)? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 100 MHz
About 200 MHz
About 50 MHz
laser-013.explanation: In a mode-locked laser, a single pulse circulates in the resonator, and part of it is extracted each time it reaches the output mirror. The repetition rate is the reciprocal of the round-trip time: f = c/(2L) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 1.5) = 1.0×10⁸ Hz, or about 100 MHz. This also equals the longitudinal mode spacing. About 200 MHz divides by the one-way time, and about 50 MHz counts the round trip twice. To raise the repetition rate, shorten the resonator or use harmonic mode locking, which puts several pulses into one round trip. The longitudinal modes of a mode-locked laser form an evenly spaced “optical frequency comb”, which is also used for precision frequency measurement.

laser-014.question: Which value is closest to the spectral width of a transform-limited Gaussian pulse with a center wavelength of 800 nm and a duration (FWHM) of 100 fs? (Time-bandwidth product ΔνΔt = 0.441.)
choices: About 0.94 nm
About 94 nm
About 9.4 nm
laser-014.explanation: The frequency width is Δν = 0.441 / Δt = 0.441 / (100×10⁻¹⁵) ≈ 4.4 THz. In wavelength, Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (800×10⁻⁹)² × 4.4×10¹² / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 9.4 nm. About 0.94 nm and about 94 nm are order-of-magnitude errors. Because of the time-frequency uncertainty relation, shorter pulses need wider spectra; a 10 fs pulse needs roughly 94 nm. If the measured product exceeds 0.441, the pulse is chirped (its frequency changes in time), which indicates room to shorten it further by compensating dispersion with a prism pair or chirped mirrors.

laser-015.question: What is the main reason fiber lasers can maintain good beam quality (M²) even at high power?
choices: Because stimulated emission does not occur in fiber, and only spontaneously emitted light is guided along the core and comes out, so the beam is not disturbed
Because the transverse mode is set by the guiding structure of a single-mode core, and the long, thin shape dissipates heat well and resists thermal lensing
Because over the long fiber the light gradually shifts to a shorter wavelength with less diffraction spreading, which steadily improves the beam quality as it travels
laser-015.explanation: In a fiber laser, the core that serves as the gain medium is itself a waveguide, so the transverse mode of the output beam is set by the core's index profile; with a single-mode core, M² is close to 1. Its cross section is also tiny relative to its length, giving a large surface area for cooling, so thermal lensing (index changes from temperature gradients), a problem in solid-state laser rods, barely disturbs the beam. Being a laser, it amplifies light by stimulated emission; spontaneous emission alone cannot give high-power coherent light. The wavelength is set by the rare-earth transition (about 1.03–1.08 µm for ytterbium) and does not get shorter during propagation. The limits to higher power are nonlinear effects such as stimulated Raman scattering, and mode instability.

laser-016.question: The ratio A/B of the Einstein coefficients, which compares spontaneous and stimulated emission, is proportional to the cube of the frequency ν. Which reason for the difficulty of making short-wavelength lasers such as X-ray lasers follows from this?
choices: At higher frequency stimulated emission stops occurring altogether and only spontaneous emission remains, so light is not amplified in the cavity
At higher frequency spontaneous emission is faster and empties the upper level quickly, so sustaining an inversion requires extremely strong pumping
At higher frequency each photon carries less energy, so more photons are needed for the same output power and the pumping cannot keep up
laser-016.explanation: Comparison with the blackbody radiation formula gives A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³ (for a refractive index of 1), so for the same stimulated-emission coefficient, spontaneous emission grows as the cube of frequency. At short wavelengths the upper-level lifetime becomes extremely short and atoms quickly drop by spontaneous emission, so the pumping needed to keep an inversion rises steeply with frequency. This is why X-ray lasers need enormous pumping or a free-electron laser. Stimulated emission does not stop occurring. The photon energy hν increases with frequency, so saying it decreases is backward.

laser-017.question: A laser has a 0.5 m cavity with one mirror of 100% reflectance, an output mirror of 90% reflectance and an internal loss in the gain medium of 0.05 /m. Which value is closest to the threshold gain coefficient g_th = α + (1/(2L)) ln(1/(R₁R₂))?
choices: About 0.16 /m
About 0.11 /m
About 0.26 /m
laser-017.explanation: In one round trip the light is multiplied by exp(2gL) from gain, exp(−2αL) from internal loss and R₁R₂ from the two mirrors, and threshold is the condition that this product equals exactly 1. Taking logarithms gives g_th = α + (1/(2L)) ln(1/(R₁R₂)) = 0.05 + ln(1/0.9)/(2 × 0.5) = 0.05 + 0.105 ≈ 0.16 /m. About 0.11 /m leaves out the internal loss, and about 0.26 /m forgets the factor 2 for the round trip, doubling the mirror loss. Lowering the output-mirror reflectance extracts more light but also raises the threshold, so there is an optimum reflectance that maximizes output.

laser-018.question: In a continuous-wave laser, the pumping is raised from twice to three times the threshold. Which correctly describes the steady-state gain (population inversion) of the gain medium and the output?
choices: The gain rises in proportion to the pumping by a factor of 1.5, and the output grows explosively as an exponential of the gain
Neither the gain nor the output changes, and all of the additional pumping is lost as spontaneous emission and heat
The gain stays fixed at its threshold value, and the additional pumping goes into increasing the output light
laser-018.explanation: Above threshold, the light in the cavity grows by the amount the gain exceeds the loss, and stimulated emission driven by that light depletes the inversion. In steady state the system settles where the round-trip gain exactly equals the loss, so the gain is clamped at its threshold value and the extra pumping becomes extra photons in the cavity, that is, more output. The output therefore rises roughly in proportion to the pumping above threshold, and the slope is the slope efficiency. If the gain kept rising with the pumping, the light would grow without limit on each round trip and no steady state would exist. Most of the extra pumping goes into stimulated emission, so it is not all lost.

laser-019.question: Regarding the width of the gain spectrum of a gas laser such as the He-Ne laser (about 1.5 GHz wide at 632.8 nm), which pairing of the main cause and the type of broadening is correct?
choices: The natural width set by the level lifetimes, a homogeneous broadening in which every atom has the same broad line shape
Doppler shifts from the thermal motion of atoms, an inhomogeneous broadening in which atoms of different velocities cover different frequencies
Pressure broadening from collisions between atoms, an inhomogeneous broadening in which atoms of different velocities cover different frequencies
laser-019.explanation: The neon atoms in the discharge tube are in thermal motion, and the Doppler effect shifts each atom's transition frequency according to its velocity component along the beam. The result is inhomogeneous broadening, with different atoms covering different frequencies, and its width of about 1.5 GHz is far larger than the natural width set by the lifetimes of the upper and lower levels (tens of MHz or less). The natural width is a homogeneous broadening shared by all atoms and is not the main cause here. Collisional pressure broadening is also homogeneous and is small in a low-pressure discharge tube. In an inhomogeneously broadened medium, light at one frequency depletes the inversion of only some of the atoms, so several longitudinal modes can easily oscillate at once.

laser-020.question: An Nd:YAG laser oscillating at 1064 nm is pumped by an 808 nm diode laser. If each pump photon yields one laser photon, which value is closest to the upper limit of the energy conversion efficiency (the value set by the quantum efficiency)?
choices: About 76%
About 24%
100% (no loss, because the number of photons is conserved)
laser-020.explanation: Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so the energy ratio of one pump photon (808 nm) to the one laser photon it yields (1064 nm) is 808/1064 ≈ 0.76, giving an upper limit of about 76%. The remaining 24% or so goes into lattice vibrations during relaxation from the pump level to the upper laser level and from the lower laser level to the ground state, and becomes heat as the quantum defect. About 24% is the fraction turned into heat, mistaken for the efficiency. Even if the photon number is conserved, each photon carries less energy, so the efficiency cannot be 100%. Combinations with a small quantum defect, such as Yb:YAG pumped at 940 nm and lasing at 1030 nm, generate less heat and suit high-power operation.

laser-021.question: In a He-Ne laser, the frequency range over which the gain exceeds the loss is about 1.5 GHz, and the mirror spacing is 1.0 m. Which value is closest to the number of longitudinal modes that can oscillate simultaneously? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s; take the refractive index inside the cavity as 1.)
choices: About 1
About 5
About 10
laser-021.explanation: The longitudinal mode spacing is Δν = c/(2L) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 1.0) = 150 MHz, so the number of modes within the 1.5 GHz range where the gain exceeds the loss is 1.5×10⁹ / 150×10⁶ ≈ 10. About 5 ignores the round trip and takes the spacing as c/L = 300 MHz. About 1 reflects the misconception that a laser always oscillates at a single frequency; when the gain range holds several mode spacings, several longitudinal modes can oscillate at once. Because the He-Ne gain is inhomogeneously broadened, it is especially prone to multimode operation. Single-longitudinal-mode operation is obtained by shortening the cavity so that the mode spacing approaches the gain width, or by selecting just one mode with an intracavity etalon.

laser-022.question: A laser with a pump threshold of 2.0 W and a slope efficiency of 40% (the ratio of the increase in output to the increase in pump power above threshold) is operated at a pump power of 7.0 W. Which value is closest to its output power?
choices: About 2.0 W
About 2.8 W
About 0.8 W
laser-022.explanation: Above threshold, the output increases almost linearly with pump power: P_out = η_s (P_p − P_th) = 0.40 × (7.0 − 2.0) = 2.0 W. About 2.8 W is 0.40 × 7.0 without subtracting the threshold; it overlooks the fact that the pump power up to threshold is spent creating the population inversion and compensating the cavity loss, and contributes nothing to the output. About 0.8 W is 0.40 × 7.0 − 2.0, subtracting the pump threshold after multiplying by the efficiency. The overall (optical-to-optical) efficiency here is 2.0/7.0 ≈ 29%, smaller than the slope efficiency. The upper limit of the slope efficiency is set by the quantum efficiency and by the fraction of light extracted through the output coupler.

laser-023.question: In a linear cavity, where a standing wave forms between two mirrors, several longitudinal modes often oscillate simultaneously even when the gain medium is homogeneously broadened. Which is the main reason?
choices: Even in a homogeneously broadened medium each atom handles a different frequency, so each longitudinal mode oscillates using the population inversion of different atoms
At the nodes of the standing wave the population inversion is left unused, and another longitudinal mode with antinodes at those positions can oscillate using the remaining gain
The reflectance of a dielectric mirror differs greatly from one longitudinal mode to the next, so only the few modes with high reflectance are selected and oscillate together
laser-023.explanation: The intensity of a standing wave alternates between antinodes and nodes along the cavity, so the oscillating mode uses only the population inversion at its antinodes and leaves gain unused at its nodes. This is called spatial hole burning. A longitudinal mode at a slightly different frequency has its antinodes and nodes in shifted positions, so it can oscillate using the remaining gain. A ring cavity, in which light circulates in one direction, forms no standing wave, which suppresses this effect and allows single-longitudinal-mode operation. Different atoms handling different frequencies is the property of inhomogeneous broadening; with homogeneous broadening every atom provides common gain to all modes. The reflectance of a dielectric mirror hardly changes between adjacent longitudinal modes.

laser-024.question: The output beam of an edge-emitting semiconductor laser has an elongated elliptical cross section and spreads widely in the direction perpendicular to the active layer (sometimes more than 20° half-angle). Which correctly explains why?
choices: The active layer has a lower refractive index than its surroundings, so light is pushed out of it and refracts to spread in the perpendicular direction
Stimulated emission is strong in the direction parallel to the active layer and spontaneous emission dominates in the perpendicular direction, so the perpendicular spread is larger
The emitting region is only about 1 µm across in the direction perpendicular to the active layer, close to the wavelength, and a smaller aperture spreads more by diffraction
laser-024.explanation: The emitting region at the facet is elongated, about 1 µm thick perpendicular to the active layer and several µm wide parallel to it, so the diffraction divergence (roughly λ/(πw₀)) differs greatly between the two directions. The axis that spreads strongly, along the small perpendicular dimension, is called the fast axis, and the parallel direction is the slow axis. For this reason the beam is reshaped into a circular one with cylindrical lenses or anamorphic prisms before fiber coupling or focusing. A vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL), which emits from its surface, has a circular aperture several µm or more across and so produces a circular beam with small divergence. The active layer has a higher refractive index than its surroundings in order to confine the light. The ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission is not what determines the beam shape.

laser-025.question: In gas lasers with external mirrors (such as He-Ne lasers), the windows at both ends of the discharge tube are sometimes mounted tilted at the Brewster angle to the optical axis. Which correctly describes the effect?
choices: p-polarized light passes the windows without reflection loss, while s-polarized light is lost by reflection on every round trip, so the output is linearly polarized
Reflection at the window surfaces becomes zero for all polarizations, so the loss of an unpolarized output is reduced without anti-reflection coatings
Refraction at the windows tilts the light relative to the axis, so a transverse mode is selected on every round trip and the output is circularly polarized
laser-025.explanation: At the Brewster angle the reflectance for p-polarized light, parallel to the plane of incidence, is zero, so p-polarized light passes the windows without loss. For s-polarized light, perpendicular to the plane of incidence, glass with an index of 1.5 reflects about 15% per surface out of the cavity, so in a low-gain gas laser s-polarized oscillation is suppressed and the output is linearly p-polarized. The reflection vanishes only for p polarization, not for all polarizations. A window is a plane-parallel plate, so the light leaves parallel to its original direction, which has nothing to do with transverse-mode selection or circular polarization. Another advantage is that the windows need no anti-reflection coating, avoiding coating damage and degradation from the discharge.

laser-026.question: A linear cavity in air is 0.30 m long; one mirror has a reflectance of 100% and the output mirror 98% (no other losses). Which value is closest to the photon lifetime in the cavity, τc = 2L / (c × (−ln R₁R₂))? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 99 ns
About 2.0 ns
About 50 ns
laser-026.explanation: The round-trip time is 2L/c = 0.60 m / (3.0×10⁸ m/s) = 2.0 ns, and the fraction lost per round trip is −ln(1.00 × 0.98) ≈ 0.0202. τc = 2.0 ns / 0.0202 ≈ 99 ns, so a photon stays in the cavity for about 50 round trips. About 2.0 ns is the round-trip time without dividing by the loss. About 50 ns divides the one-way time L/c, rather than the round-trip time, by the loss. The photon lifetime sets the cavity mode linewidth Δν = 1/(2πτc) (about 1.6 MHz here) and how quickly a Q-switched pulse builds up. Lowering the output-mirror reflectance extracts a larger fraction of the light but shortens the photon lifetime.

laser-027.question: A Q-switched laser emits pulses of 10 mJ energy and 10 ns duration at a repetition rate of 10 Hz. Which combination of average power and peak power is closest? (Estimate the peak power as energy divided by pulse duration.)
choices: Average power 1 mW, peak power about 1 MW
Average power 0.1 W, peak power about 1 MW
Average power 0.1 W, peak power about 1 kW
laser-027.explanation: The average power is the energy per second: 10 mJ × 10 Hz = 0.1 W. The peak power is the output during the pulse: 10×10⁻³ J / 10×10⁻⁹ s = 1×10⁶ W, about 1 MW. Although the average is only 0.1 W, the light is concentrated into 10 ns, so the instantaneous power is ten million times the average. This is why Q-switched lasers are used for materials processing and nonlinear optics. About 1 kW confuses ns with µs. 1 mW is the number obtained by dividing 10 mJ by 10 Hz, but J ÷ Hz has units of J·s, not a power in W; the pulse energy must be multiplied by the repetition rate to give the energy per second. The ratio of peak to average power is the inverse of the duty cycle, the pulse duration divided by the repetition period.

laser-028.question: Why does a distributed-feedback (DFB) semiconductor laser, used as a light source in optical communications, oscillate readily in a single longitudinal mode, unlike a Fabry–Pérot semiconductor laser?
choices: Its cavity is made extremely short, a few µm, so the longitudinal mode spacing exceeds the gain width and only one mode falls within the gain
It uses a special material whose gain spectrum is over 100 times narrower than in Fabry–Pérot lasers, so only one mode is amplified in the first place
A grating of period Λ along the active layer strongly feeds back only wavelengths satisfying the Bragg condition λ = 2n_effΛ
laser-028.explanation: In a DFB laser, an index grating of period Λ runs alongside the active layer, giving reflection distributed over the whole cavity length. Only a narrow range of wavelengths satisfying the Bragg condition λ = 2n_effΛ is strongly fed back, so within the gain width the low-loss mode is narrowed to one (in practice a λ/4 phase shift at the grating center selects a single mode). For example, n_eff = 3.2 and Λ ≈ 242 nm give 1550 nm. The gain width is set by the material and is tens of nm in a DFB laser, just as in a Fabry–Pérot laser. Making the cavity extremely short so that only one longitudinal mode fits is the approach of the vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL); a DFB cavity is hundreds of µm long.

laser-029.question: Placing a circular aperture of suitable size inside the cavity of a solid-state laser makes it easier to obtain a fundamental transverse mode (TEM₀₀, Gaussian) output beam. Which explains why?
choices: Higher-order transverse modes spread wider than the fundamental mode, so they suffer large losses at the aperture and only the fundamental mode exceeds threshold
Light diffracted at the aperture edge interferes and reshapes the intensity distribution in the cavity into a Gaussian, converting every transverse mode into TEM₀₀ as it passes
Passing the aperture shortens the wavelength and reduces the divergence, so higher-order modes become beams with the same spread as the fundamental mode
laser-029.explanation: Transverse modes are standing-wave patterns with different cross-sectional intensity distributions; the TEM₀₀ Gaussian beam is the narrowest, and higher-order modes extend farther out. An aperture in the cavity imposes a large loss at its edge on the wider higher-order modes on every round trip, while the loss of the fundamental mode stays small. Modes whose loss exceeds the gain do not oscillate, so only the fundamental mode remains. If the aperture is too small the fundamental mode also suffers loss and the output drops, so it is chosen slightly larger than the beam radius. The aperture does not reshape the modes; it selects among them by their difference in loss. Nor does passing through an aperture change the wavelength.

laser-030.question: Gain media with a long upper-laser-level lifetime are suited to obtaining high-energy Q-switched pulses (about 230 µs for Nd:YAG). Which explains why?
choices: A longer upper-level lifetime gives a larger stimulated-emission cross section, so the gain is higher when the Q-switch opens and the pulse is shorter
While the cavity loss is held high to stop lasing, the pump energy is stored as population inversion, and with a short lifetime it is lost to spontaneous emission
The upper-level lifetime directly sets the pulse duration, so a longer-lived medium gives longer pulses and correspondingly more pulse energy
laser-030.explanation: In Q-switching, the cavity loss is first held high to prevent lasing while pumping continues, building up an inversion far above threshold. When the loss is suddenly lowered, the stored energy is extracted all at once as a short pulse of the order of ns. During storage the upper level still decays by spontaneous emission with lifetime τ, so if τ is shorter than the pumping time the inversion saturates and energy cannot be accumulated. Nd:YAG has about 230 µs, whereas carrier lifetimes in semiconductor lasers are of the order of ns, so they can store almost nothing. The pulse duration is set mainly by the cavity photon lifetime and the gain, not by the upper-level lifetime. Also, media with longer upper-level lifetimes tend, if anything, to have smaller stimulated-emission cross sections.

laser-031.question: For the 1064 nm laser transition of Nd:YAG, take the stimulated-emission cross section as σ = 2.8×10⁻¹⁹ cm² and the upper-level lifetime as τ = 230 µs. Which value is closest to the gain saturation intensity of this four-level system, I_sat = hν/(στ)? (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 29 W/cm²
About 2.9 mW/cm²
About 2.9 kW/cm²
laser-031.explanation: The photon energy is hν = hc/λ = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 3.0×10⁸ / 1.064×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.87×10⁻¹⁹ J. Then I_sat = 1.87×10⁻¹⁹ / (2.8×10⁻¹⁹ cm² × 230×10⁻⁶ s) ≈ 2.9×10³ W/cm², about 2.9 kW/cm². The saturation intensity is the intensity at which stimulated emission depletes the upper level as fast as its natural lifetime does, and at this intensity a homogeneously broadened gain falls to half its small-signal value. About 2.9 mW/cm² divides by the bare number 230 instead of 230×10⁻⁶ s, and about 29 W/cm² comes from entering the wavelength in centimeters (1.064×10⁻⁴ cm) to match the cross section while keeping c in m/s, which makes the photon energy 100 times too small.

laser-032.question: A Gaussian beam of radius w (the radius at which the intensity falls to 1/e² of its central value) is passed, centered, through a circular aperture of radius w. Which value is closest to the fraction of the power transmitted? (Take the fraction of power inside a circle of radius r as 1 − exp(−2r²/w²).)
choices: About 86%
About 63%
About 50%
laser-032.explanation: Setting r = w gives 1 − e⁻² ≈ 0.865, so about 86% of the power passes through and the remaining 14% lies in the wings outside the 1/e² radius. About 63% is 1 − e⁻¹, obtained by dropping the factor 2 in the exponent; that fraction lies inside a radius of w/√2, within the 1/e² radius. About 50% assumes that half the power lies inside the radius; half the power is actually contained within r ≈ 0.59w. Clipping the wings with an aperture produces diffraction ripples, so to pass nearly all of the power (about 99%) the aperture radius is made at least about 1.5w. When a beam size is quoted as a 1/e² diameter, it helps to remember that about 86% of the power lies inside it.

laser-033.question: As the temperature of a Fabry–Perot semiconductor laser is raised, its lasing wavelength drifts slowly toward longer wavelengths and occasionally jumps (mode hopping). Which explanation of this behavior is correct?
choices: Thermal expansion shortens the cavity and widens the mode spacing, so fewer modes fit under the gain peak and lasing jumps to a remaining mode
The gain peak shifts quickly to longer wavelengths as the bandgap shrinks, while the modes shift slowly with the index, so the peak moves to the next mode
The gain peak shifts to shorter wavelengths while the modes shift to longer ones, so lasing jumps to another mode whenever the two move apart
laser-033.explanation: The bandgap of a semiconductor shrinks with temperature, so the peak of the gain spectrum moves relatively quickly toward longer wavelengths. The wavelength of each longitudinal mode, by contrast, is set by the optical length nL of the cavity and lengthens only slowly through the small rise in index and thermal expansion. Lasing occurs on the mode closest to the gain peak, so as the temperature rises the wavelength first follows that mode slowly, and when the peak has moved close to the neighbouring mode, lasing hops over and the wavelength jumps. Thermal expansion lengthens rather than shortens the cavity, so the claim of a widening mode spacing is wrong, and a gain peak moving to shorter wavelengths has the direction reversed. In a DFB laser the wavelength is fixed by the grating, so only the slow drift remains.

laser-034.question: A titanium-sapphire (Ti:Al₂O₃) laser can be tuned over a wide range of about 700–1000 nm and can also produce ultrashort pulses of around 10 fs. Which is the correct reason its gain bandwidth is so wide?
choices: Ti³⁺ has many sharp levels, and many transitions at slightly different wavelengths occur at once, so densely packed narrow lines form a broad band
The Ti³⁺ ions move rapidly by thermal motion in the crystal, so the Doppler effect shifts each ion's wavelength, giving wider inhomogeneous broadening than in gas lasers
The Ti³⁺ transition is vibronic, coupled to lattice vibrations whose levels overlap almost continuously, so the gain spans a wide range
laser-034.explanation: The energy of the Ti³⁺ d electron depends strongly on the arrangement of the surrounding oxygen ions, so electronic transitions are accompanied by excitation of lattice vibrations (vibronic transitions). Because the vibrational levels overlap almost continuously, absorption spreads around 500 nm in the blue-green and emission over about 650–1100 nm, giving a broad, continuous gain band. This bandwidth makes both wide tunability and, through the time–bandwidth product, ultrashort pulses possible. A set of sharp lines resembles the transitions of rare-earth ions, whose electrons are shielded by outer shells, and does not apply to Ti³⁺. Ions in a crystal are fixed in the lattice, so there is no gas-like Doppler broadening. Since the absorption lies in the blue-green, the laser is pumped with green lasers such as 532 nm sources.

laser-035.question: When pumping of a solid-state laser such as Nd:YAG is switched on suddenly, the output does not become steady at once but oscillates in spikes that decay before settling to a steady value (relaxation oscillations). Which explanation of this behavior is correct?
choices: When the light builds up suddenly it depletes the inversion, and when the light decays the inversion grows again; this exchange oscillates because the upper-level lifetime is longer than the photon lifetime
Several longitudinal modes lase at once, and the beats at their frequency differences make the output rise and fall, so the spikes are spaced by the beat period
Ripple in the pump power supply passes directly to the gain and modulates the output at the supply period, so stabilizing the pump removes the spikes completely
laser-035.explanation: Just before lasing starts, the inversion has built up well above threshold, so the photon number rises abruptly and drives the inversion below threshold. The photons then decay, the pump restores the inversion, and the light builds up again. In solid-state lasers, where the upper-level lifetime (about 230 µs in Nd:YAG) is much longer than the cavity photon lifetime (of order ns), this exchange becomes a damped oscillation seen as spikes spaced by a few to tens of µs. Beats between longitudinal modes occur at their frequency differences (hundreds of MHz to GHz), a much faster variation. Ripple in the power supply is unrelated; the spikes occur even with a stable pump. In many gas lasers, whose upper-level lifetime is not long compared with the photon lifetime, relaxation oscillations are hardly seen.

laser-036.question: The threshold current of a semiconductor laser is often written as I_th = I₀ exp(T/T₀) using the characteristic temperature T₀. For a laser with T₀ = 60 K, by roughly what factor does the threshold current increase when the temperature is raised from 25 °C to 55 °C?
choices: About 1.5 times
About 1.65 times
About 1.41 times
laser-036.explanation: The threshold ratio is exp(ΔT/T₀) = exp(30/60) = e^0.5 ≈ 1.65. Only the temperature difference matters, so the result is the same whether one works in °C or K. About 1.5 times approximates the exponential by its first-order term, 1 + ΔT/T₀, which is inaccurate at ΔT/T₀ = 0.5. About 1.41 times treats T₀ as the temperature rise that doubles the threshold, giving 2^(30/60); in fact a rise of T₀ multiplies the threshold by e ≈ 2.7. Lasers with a small T₀ are more temperature-sensitive and need temperature control or an active region with deeper carrier confinement.

laser-037.question: A semiconductor laser emitting at 980 nm has a slope efficiency (the slope of optical output versus current above threshold) of 0.80 W/A. Which value is closest to its external differential quantum efficiency (the number of additional photons emitted per additional injected electron)? (Take hc/q ≈ 1.24 eV·µm.)
choices: About 80%
About 100%
About 63%
laser-037.explanation: One photon carries hc/λ ≈ 1.24/0.98 ≈ 1.27 eV, so if every electron became an emitted photon, each ampere would produce 1.27 W of light. The external differential quantum efficiency is the actual slope divided by this value: ηd = (dP/dI) × λ[µm]/1.24 = 0.80 × 0.98/1.24 ≈ 0.63, or about 63%. About 80% reads the W/A figure directly as an efficiency; W/A is power divided by current and has the dimensions of a voltage. About 100% applies the conversion factor the wrong way round. The remainder is lost to internal absorption in the cavity, to light leaving through the facet that is not used for output, and so on.

laser-038.question: In a homogeneously broadened gain medium with small-signal gain coefficient g₀ and saturation intensity I_sat, light of intensity I reduces the gain coefficient to g = g₀/(1 + I/I_sat) (gain saturation). What is the gain coefficient when the light intensity is three times the saturation intensity (I = 3I_sat)?
choices: g₀/4
g₀/3
g₀/2
laser-038.explanation: g = g₀/(1 + 3) = g₀/4. The gain halves at I = I_sat and falls roughly in inverse proportion to the intensity above that. g₀/3 drops the 1 in the denominator, giving g₀I_sat/I, an approximation valid only for very strong light, applied here at just three times I_sat. g₀/2 uses the inhomogeneous-broadening formula g₀/√(1 + I/I_sat). In an inhomogeneously broadened medium, only the atoms resonant with the light's frequency saturate, so the gain falls more slowly. In an oscillating laser, this saturation clamps the gain at its threshold value.

laser-039.question: Lasers with a large-aperture, high-gain medium, such as CO₂ and excimer lasers, sometimes use an unstable resonator that does not satisfy the stability condition. Why?
choices: An unstable resonator has no diffraction loss, so even a low-gain medium lases at a low threshold and no output coupler is needed
Light spreads outward on each round trip, so the mode fills the wide gain medium and a low-divergence beam is taken out around the edge of a mirror
Light converges toward the axis on each round trip, so a narrow, high-quality fundamental-mode beam saturates the gain strongly at high intensity
laser-039.explanation: The fundamental mode of a stable resonator has a size set by the mirror curvatures and spacing, of order √(λL), which is too thin to use most of a wide gain medium; enlarging the aperture lets higher-order transverse modes oscillate and degrades the beam. In an unstable resonator, rays move farther from the axis on every round trip, so the mode fills the whole cross-section of the medium, and the light spilling around a small output mirror is extracted as an annular beam. Because light escapes on every round trip, the loss is large and only high-gain media can be used, so a low threshold with low gain is the opposite of the truth. Confinement of light around the axis is the behaviour of a stable resonator.

laser-040.question: Inserting a Cr⁴⁺:YAG crystal into the cavity of an Nd:YAG laser produces Q-switched pulses without any electrical drive (passive Q-switching). How does it work?
choices: Cr⁴⁺:YAG is a Kerr medium whose index depends on intensity; it focuses only strong light through an aperture like a lens, lowering the loss and producing a pulse
Cr⁴⁺:YAG is a second gain medium that amplifies 1064 nm light; with two stages of gain the light builds up suddenly and a pulse is emitted
Cr⁴⁺:YAG is a saturable absorber: once inversion has built up and the light grows, its absorption saturates and the loss drops abruptly
laser-040.explanation: A saturable absorber absorbs weak light, but under strong light its absorbing lower level empties and it becomes nearly transparent. At first its absorption loss prevents lasing while pumping builds up the inversion. When the gain exceeds the loss and light starts to grow, the absorber saturates, the loss drops abruptly, and the stored energy is released at once as a short pulse. The repetition rate is set by the pump power, and the inability to trigger the pulse externally is what distinguishes passive from active Q-switching. An intensity-dependent index is the mechanism of Kerr-lens mode-locking, and Cr⁴⁺:YAG is not a gain medium that amplifies 1064 nm light either.

laser-041.question: A vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL) has distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) with reflectances above 99% above and below the active layer. Why does it need a reflectance far higher than the facet reflectance of an edge-emitting laser (about 30%)?
choices: Because the cavity is short and the longitudinal mode spacing is narrow, so unless the reflectance is raised to strongly suppress neighboring modes, the laser oscillates on many longitudinal modes
Because the light is emitted perpendicular to the active layer, so unless the reflectance is raised to spread the light sideways along the layer, the beam becomes elliptical instead of circular
Because the light passes through only a few tens of nanometers of active layer with gain, so the gain per round trip is tiny and the laser cannot oscillate unless the losses are kept very small
laser-041.explanation: In a VCSEL the light travels back and forth perpendicular to the layers, so in one round trip it passes through only a few tens of nanometers of quantum wells with gain, and the round-trip gain is only about 1%. To oscillate, the round-trip loss must be smaller than this gain, so the mirror reflectance is made 99% or higher. DBRs of a few tens of pairs of semiconductor layers with different refractive indices achieve this. In an edge-emitting laser the light travels along an active layer hundreds of micrometers long, so the gain is sufficient even with cleaved facets of about 30% reflectance. The VCSEL cavity is only a few micrometers long and its longitudinal mode spacing is wide, so it tends to oscillate on a single longitudinal mode; the explanation about suppressing neighboring modes has it backward. The circular beam is determined by the shape of the emitting area, not by the reflectance.

laser-042.question: In a continuous-wave laser, the output power was measured while changing only the transmittance of the output mirror, with the gain medium and pumping unchanged. The output was maximum at a certain transmittance and decreased for both larger and smaller transmittances. Which explains this?
choices: A smaller transmittance makes the light inside the cavity stronger and raises the output, but too strong a field deforms the mirror thermally, so there is an optimum transmittance set by heating
With a small transmittance most of the light is lost to internal losses, and with a large one the threshold rises and the intracavity light weakens, so an optimum lies in between
The output increases in proportion to the transmittance, but beyond a certain value the output mirror passes too much light, disturbing the polarization so that the output drops suddenly
laser-042.explanation: The output is the product of the intracavity intensity and the transmittance of the output mirror. Reducing the transmittance strengthens the intracavity light, but only a small fraction is extracted, and much of the light is lost to internal losses such as absorption and scattering in the medium. Increasing the transmittance extracts a larger fraction, but the round-trip loss rises, the threshold goes up, the gain margin shrinks and the intracavity light weakens, until oscillation finally stops. There is therefore an optimum transmittance determined by the small-signal gain and the internal loss. Thermal deformation of mirrors can be a separate problem at high power, but it is not the reason for this optimum. The transmittance does not disturb the polarization either.

laser-043.question: Excimer lasers such as KrF (248 nm) and ArF (193 nm) make population inversion easy to achieve. Which is the main reason?
choices: The lower laser level is a state in which the atoms repel each other, so the molecules dissociate immediately and the lower level is always empty
Rare gases and halogens form strongly bound, stable molecules in the ground state, so many molecules occupy the upper level even in thermal equilibrium
The upper level has a lifetime of several milliseconds, longer than in solid-state lasers, so the discharge energy can be stored for a long time to build a large inversion
laser-043.explanation: An excimer (excited dimer) is a molecule that forms from a rare gas and a halogen only when they are in an excited state. The ground state into which it falls when emitting light is a repulsive, unbound state, so the molecule immediately falls apart and does not accumulate in the lower level. Therefore even a small number of molecules in the upper level produces a population inversion. Since there is no stable molecule in the ground state, the explanation about many molecules in the upper level in equilibrium is backward. The upper-level lifetime is short, of the order of a few nanoseconds, so energy cannot be stored for long and the gas is excited by a strong, short discharge. Because the lower level is unbound, the emission is broad; these lasers are used for lithography (exposure) in semiconductor manufacturing and for materials processing.

laser-044.question: In a laser whose gain exceeds the loss over a frequency range of 30 GHz, a parallel-plate etalon of fused silica (refractive index 1.45) is placed in the cavity to select a single longitudinal mode. To have only one etalon transmission peak within the gain range, the etalon's free spectral range (FSR = c/(2nt), where t is the thickness) should be at least 30 GHz. Which is closest to the maximum etalon thickness? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 6.9 mm
About 5.0 mm
About 3.4 mm
laser-044.explanation: From c/(2nt) ≥ 30 GHz, t ≤ c/(2n × 30 GHz) = 3.0×10⁸/(2 × 1.45 × 3.0×10¹⁰) ≈ 3.4×10⁻³ m, or about 3.4 mm. If the etalon is thicker, its FSR becomes narrower than the gain range, gain remains at another etalon transmission peak, and the laser can oscillate at a distant frequency as well. About 6.9 mm forgets the 2 for the round trip and uses c/(nt). About 5.0 mm forgets the refractive index and treats the path as if it were in vacuum. Conversely, if the etalon is too thin, its transmission peaks become broad and cannot distinguish neighboring longitudinal modes of the cavity, so the thickness and finesse are chosen to satisfy both conditions. The selected frequency is tuned by tilting the etalon or changing its temperature.

laser-045.question: In a He-Ne laser with a wavelength of 632.8 nm and a cavity length of 0.30 m, a temperature change lengthens the cavity by 0.10 µm. Which is closest to the magnitude of the change in the oscillation frequency of one longitudinal mode? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s; take Δν/ν = ΔL/L.)
choices: About 320 MHz
About 160 MHz
About 170 Hz
laser-045.explanation: The oscillation frequency is ν = c/λ ≈ 4.74×10¹⁴ Hz, and the frequency of a longitudinal mode is inversely proportional to the length, so Δν = ν × ΔL/L = 4.74×10¹⁴ × (0.10×10⁻⁶/0.30) ≈ 1.6×10⁸ Hz: the frequency falls by about 160 MHz. This is about one third of the mode spacing c/(2L) = 500 MHz; a length change of λ/2 = 316 nm moves the mode exactly to the position of its neighbor. About 320 MHz wrongly doubles the result for the round trip, but the ratio ΔL/L is already the ratio of the round-trip paths. About 170 Hz multiplies by the 500 MHz mode spacing instead of ν. Because even slight thermal expansion moves the frequency this much, frequency-stable lasers use cavities made of low-expansion materials and feedback control of the length.
